morning_d1.text: Gannet Rock, this is Station Penobscot, radio check. Tide's dropping fast. If you want the outer stacks before noon, now's your window. Say something, Arthur, so I know the set works.
morning_d1.speaker: clara

options.text: Penobscot, Gannet Rock. Lamp's steady, weights wound. I've also located the coffee, which seemed the main thing.
options.reply: Copy, that is the main thing. Give me a shout if anything strange washed up in last night's squall.

options.text: Copy. I'll look around and radio if there's anything worth your time.
options.reply: Worth my time is a low bar at this hour, Arthur. Anything you find, I'd like to hear about.

react_east_bar_first.text: East bar. Watch in your hand, Arthur, not in your pocket. It's a long walk back when the water turns.
react_east_bar_first.speaker: clara

react_west_bar_first.text: West bar's narrower than the east, and it floods first. Mind the gullies.
react_west_bar_first.speaker: clara

react_bar_rising.text: Water's making. You've maybe an hour of crossing left. I'd start back.
react_bar_rising.speaker: clara

react_bar_closing.text: Arthur. Get off that bar. Now. I mean it.
react_bar_closing.speaker: clara

react_west_withheld.text: You're on the west stack now. Anything from the east stack you'd like to put on the record?
react_west_withheld.speaker: clara

options.text: There was a canister in the hull. PROJECT PELAGIC, 1974. I should have said.
options.reply: Yes. You should have. Thank you for saying it now.

options.text: Not yet. I'd like to understand it first.
options.reply: I know that one. All right, Arthur. Whenever you're ready.

react_cottage_curious.text: Quiet in there, teacher. Have you eaten?
react_cottage_curious.speaker: clara

shipwreck.text: You've been out on the East Stack a while. What's in the hull?
shipwreck.speaker: clara

options.text: An orange canister, stamped PROJECT PELAGIC, 1974. It's in the satchel.
options.reply: ...Keep it dry and bring it back before the bar floods. Don't open it out in the salt spray.

options.text: An old trawler. Rust and rope. Nothing to report.
options.reply: Mm. Mind the water behind you. That bar goes fast.

seacave.text: Echo Cave? Your signal's bouncing off the walls. What's sitting in the arch?
seacave.speaker: clara

options.text: A rusted acoustic buoy. The casing's warm, and there's a cassette taped inside the hatch.
options.reply: Warm. ...That'll be the cold, probably. Metal does odd things. Bring the tape home, Arthur, and head for high ground.

options.text: Kelp and barnacles. It's eerie in here, that's all.
options.reply: Don't linger. The Atlantic doesn't wait for anyone enjoying the acoustics.

evening_d1.text: Beam looks beautiful from here. Thank you for telling me about that canister, Arthur. People don't always, when it's something odd.
evening_d1.speaker: clara

options.text: It said PROJECT PELAGIC on the side. Does that mean anything to you?
options.reply: ...Not tonight. I'll tell you what I can, when I can.

options.text: Just doing the job.
options.reply: Then you're better at it than the last three keepers.

evening_d1.text: Lamp's turning well. You were out on the east stack a long time today. Anything you'd care to tell me?
evening_d1.speaker: clara

options.text: There was a canister in the hull. PROJECT PELAGIC, 1974. I should have said.
options.reply: Yes. You should have. Thank you for saying it now.

options.text: Nothing worth a radio call.
options.reply: All right. Goodnight, Arthur.

evening_d1.text: Beam's turning pretty from here. How was your first day on the rock, really?
evening_d1.speaker: clara

options.text: Quieter than I expected. I'm still deciding what I think about that.
options.reply: That's honest. Most keepers say it takes three days to stop listening for company.

options.text: Busy. A great deal to log.
options.reply: All business. Fine. Get some sleep.

morning_d2.text: Slept better than I have in weeks. Funny what one straight answer does. How's the rock?
morning_d2.speaker: clara

options.text: Quiet night. Where do you want me today?
options.reply: West stack, if the water allows. The old echo cave. Mind the tide table.

options.text: That canister's still on my mind.
options.reply: Leave it dry and don't pry at it. I mean that kindly.

morning_d2.text: Morning. Fog's lifting. I'll say this once, Arthur: I'd rather you were straight with me about what's out there.
morning_d2.speaker: clara

options.text: I'll do better. I'm out of practice at being asked.
options.reply: That's all I ask.

options.text: I'm doing my job, Clara.
options.reply: Then do it well.

morning_d2.text: Morning, Arthur. Flat calm and grey out here. Anything strange wash up overnight?
morning_d2.speaker: clara

options.text: Quiet night. Lamp held.
options.reply: Good. Keep it that way.

options.text: That canister's still bothering me.
options.reply: Leave it dry and don't pry at it. I mean that kindly.

evening_d2.text: You've been quiet all evening. Did you play the tape?
evening_d2.speaker: clara

options.text: It's a man talking to his wife. June. He says the Navy lied about the cable job. He says it very politely.
options.reply: ...Yes. I know the name. Another night, Arthur. I'll tell you another night.

options.text: Just static and wind.
options.reply: Static and wind. Of course. Goodnight.

evening_d2.text: Did you find a tape out there? You've got a cassette player in the cottage.
evening_d2.speaker: clara

options.text: I'll play it tonight.
options.reply: Do. And tell me what's on it.

options.text: No tape, Clara.
options.reply: ...All right.

evening_d2.text: How was the day, Arthur? You sound far away.
evening_d2.speaker: clara

options.text: Tired. I'd forgotten how long a day is when nobody's asking you questions.
options.reply: It does that. Sleep.

options.text: Fine. Nothing to report.
options.reply: Goodnight, then.

cable.text: North cove? That's the old cable landing. The charts show a line coming ashore there. What's it look like?
cable.speaker: clara

options.text: An armored cable running straight into the sea. Brass tag: PELAGIC, ARRAY 2, USN.
options.reply: ...Then the charts weren't wrong. Leave the hut alone, Arthur, and don't touch the splice.

options.text: Rocks and kelp, mostly.
options.reply: All right. Mind the tide on the way back.

vault.text: The reef is open? I can hear the water around you. What's down there?
vault.speaker: clara

options.text: A cable vault. Salt-crusted hatch, and a field recorder wedged behind the ladder. Initials: J.H.
options.reply: ...Bring it up. Please. Then get off the reef.

options.text: Nothing. Just flooded concrete.
options.reply: Then come home.

react_north_cove_first.text: North cove. Careful on the shingle; it's slick, and the water floods that bar before the others.
react_north_cove_first.speaker: clara

react_south_reef_first.text: The reef. I've never seen it dry. You've got an hour at best, Arthur. One hour. I'm holding you to the table.
react_south_reef_first.speaker: clara

react_reef_closing.text: Arthur. The water's turned. Off the reef. Now.
react_reef_closing.speaker: clara

evening_d3.text: You found the north landing and you told me. I won't forget that, Arthur.
evening_d3.speaker: clara

options.text: What was Array 2? The tag was Navy issue.
options.reply: ...Another night. I promise.

options.text: Just doing the job.
options.reply: Then the job's in good hands.

evening_d3.text: You were in the north cove a long time. Is there something you'd like to say?
evening_d3.speaker: clara

options.text: There's a cable, and a brass tag. PELAGIC ARRAY 2. I should have said.
options.reply: Yes. You should have. Thank you.

options.text: No. I'm tired, Clara.
options.reply: All right.

evening_d3.text: Found anything in the north cove? The old charts show a cable there.
evening_d3.speaker: clara

options.text: Haven't made it up there yet.
options.reply: Fog's thick today. Wait for a clear low.

options.text: Nothing worth reporting.
options.reply: All right, Arthur.

evening_d5.text: You brought it up. Thank you, Arthur. I couldn't have gone down there.
evening_d5.speaker: clara

options.text: Whose voice is on it?
options.reply: ...Play it tonight. Then I'll answer anything you ask.

options.text: June was careful. Everything I've heard says so.
options.reply: No. She wasn't careless.

evening_d5.text: You were on the reef longer than the table allowed. What did you find?
evening_d5.speaker: clara

options.text: A recorder. A cassette, initials J.H. I'm sorry I said nothing.
options.reply: Thank you for telling me now.

options.text: Nothing, Clara.
options.reply: ...All right.

evening_d5.text: You didn't make the reef today? That low won't come again this winter.
evening_d5.speaker: clara

options.text: I'll try tomorrow.
options.reply: It will be gone by then.

options.text: It wasn't worth the risk.
options.reply: Maybe not.

morning_d3.text: Fog's down to the waterline. Listen, don't look. One strike is the north bell, two east, three south, four west. Say it back to me.
morning_d3.speaker: clara

options.text: Nineteen years of school bells. I can manage four.
options.reply: Good. Don't trust the beam in this. Trust your ears.

options.text: You worry a good deal, for a dispatcher.
options.reply: It's the job. And... other things.

morning_d3.text: Dense fog. One strike north, two east, three south, four west. Don't go out blind.
morning_d3.speaker: clara

options.text: Understood. North one, east two.
options.reply: Good.

options.text: I've been told what to do by a great many people lately.
options.reply: Then go carefully.

react_fog_bells.text: In this soup, find the bell before you trust your feet. Two strikes is the east buoy. That's the way you'd be crossing.
react_fog_bells.speaker: clara

morning_d4.text: Gale warning's up, Arthur, and the bars are done for the day. Stay by the stove. I'll be on sixteen all day. Company's allowed.
morning_d4.speaker: clara

options.text: Then I'll take the company.
options.reply: Good. I'll call you at noon.

options.text: I could still check the tower.
options.reply: On the summit, in daylight, with a rope. Not otherwise.

morning_d4.text: Gale warning's up. Bars are done for the day. Stay near the stove and keep the lamp trimmed.
morning_d4.speaker: clara

options.text: Understood. I'll sit tight.
options.reply: Good.

options.text: I could still check the tower.
options.reply: On the summit, in daylight, with a rope. Not otherwise.

midday_d4.text: Arthur, you still with me? Line's crackling. Anyone else would be climbing the walls by now.
midday_d4.speaker: clara

options.text: Snug. Lamp's trimmed, stove's roaring. Have you eaten?
options.reply: ...Toast. Don't say it.

options.text: It's too quiet in here. Tell me something. Anything.
options.reply: ...All right. Ask me anything. I'm not going anywhere in this weather either.

evening_d4.text: Long day. Storms make people talk, don't they? My father worked the Pelagic boats, Arthur. Tom Dunmore. He never said much about 1974. He was about your age that winter.
evening_d4.speaker: clara

options.text: Tell me about him.
options.reply: He'd come home smelling of diesel and salt and sit in the dark with the radio on. After '74 he stopped going out. Said the sea owed him something.

options.text: Why are you telling me now?
options.reply: Because it's blowing a gale and I'm tired of carrying it by myself.

evening_d4.text: Long day. Storms make people talk. My father worked the Pelagic boats. That's all I'll say tonight.
evening_d4.speaker: clara

options.text: Thank you for telling me.
options.reply: ...Goodnight, Arthur.

options.text: Pelagic. The canister. You knew.
options.reply: Not tonight, Arthur. Please.

options.text: Goodnight, Clara.
options.reply: Goodnight.

options.text: You're not telling me something.
options.reply: Goodnight, Arthur.

d4_why_post.text: And you? Nobody takes a winter post at forty-one without a reason.
d4_why_post.speaker: clara

options.text: My wife died in the autumn. Maren. I couldn't stay in the house.
options.reply: ...I'm sorry, Arthur. I didn't know. I'm glad you said it.

options.text: I like the quiet.
options.reply: Mm. That's not an answer, but it'll do.

morning_d5.text: Clear as glass. The tables say this is the lowest water of the winter, Arthur. My father used to say the reef opens once a decade.
morning_d5.speaker: clara

options.text: Then the south reef will be open.
options.reply: For a couple of hours at best. Watch the clock like it owes you money.

options.text: You sound nervous.
options.reply: I sound careful. There's a difference.

morning_d5.text: Clear as glass. Spring low today, the lowest water of the winter. The south reef will uncover.
morning_d5.speaker: clara

options.text: Then I'll take a look.
options.reply: Watch the clock. Keep between the poles.

options.text: Is there a reason you keep warning me?
options.reply: Habit.

morning_d6.text: Cold one. Arthur, I owe you a straight conversation. Tonight, when the lamp's lit. I wanted you to hear it from me first, so you'd know I mean it.
morning_d6.speaker: clara

options.text: I'll be listening.
options.reply: Good.

options.text: I think I already know.
options.reply: Then you know why it's hard.

morning_d6.text: Cold one. I'll try to answer what you ask tonight. I can't promise more than that.
morning_d6.speaker: clara

options.text: That's enough.
options.reply: ...Thank you.

options.text: I'd like more than trying.
options.reply: I know you would.

morning_d6.text: Cold. Don't expect much of me tonight. You've given me reasons not to.
morning_d6.speaker: clara

options.text: I know. I'm sorry.
You've given me reasons too.
options.reply: Fair.

evening_d6.text: All right. My father piloted the boat that took June Haskell to the reef. He told the Navy the table said one hour. They said two. He held off the bar with his engine running and watched the water come over it. I've kept that buoy alive ever since. I tell myself the ping is her recorder.
evening_d6.speaker: clara

options.text: That was never duty, Clara. That's grief. I know it when I see it.
options.reply: ...Yes. It is.

options.text: You could have told me on day one.
options.reply: I know. I couldn't. I didn't know you yet.

evening_d6.text: I can tell you some of it. My father was on the boats. There was an accident in '74 and the Navy buried it. I keep the buoy running because... I can't stop. That's as far as I can go tonight.
evening_d6.speaker: clara

options.text: Who was June, Clara?
options.reply: ...June Haskell. Walt's wife. Read the tapes. You'll hear the rest.

options.text: That's not the whole story.
options.reply: No. It isn't.

evening_d6.text: I don't have anything to say tonight, Arthur. You've kept things from me. I'll keep a few from you.
evening_d6.speaker: clara

options.text: I found your tape in the west buoy, Clara. Your voice. I've heard it.
options.reply: ...That wasn't yours to find. Fine. My father piloted the boat. That's all I'll say.

options.text: Then we're done talking tonight.
options.reply: Goodnight.

morning_d7.text: Last day. Funny. I've talked to you more than I talk to anyone ashore.
morning_d7.speaker: clara

options.text: Same here. I don't think I've talked this much since the classroom.
options.reply: Then we're square.

options.text: Let's finish what we started.
options.reply: Alright. Whatever you decide, I'll abide by it.

morning_d7.text: Last morning. The relief boat is due at first light tomorrow. I hope you've made up your mind.
morning_d7.speaker: clara

options.text: Nearly.
options.reply: Good.

options.text: Not yet.
options.reply: Then think carefully.

morning_d7.text: Last day. Relief boat's due at first light.
morning_d7.speaker: clara

options.text: I know.
Clara, are we all right?
options.reply: I don't know, Arthur.

evening_d7.text: Light's on. Relief boat's due at first light. You hold June's tapes, and Walt's, and my father's. Whatever you decide, I'll abide by it.
evening_d7.speaker: clara

options.text: I'm sending them to Ruth Whitcomb, in Providence. She's waited twenty-four years to hear her sister.
options.reply: ...Yes. I'll write the cover letter myself.

options.text: Let the buoy go quiet, Clara. The tapes go back in the locker. This stays between us.
options.reply: ...Then I'll cut the supply tonight. Thank you, Arthur.

evening_d7.text: Light's on. Relief boat's due at first light. You know enough to decide. What will you do?
evening_d7.speaker: clara

options.text: I'm sending the tapes to June's family. Ruth Whitcomb, in Providence.
options.reply: Do what you must. I'll sign whatever you need.

options.text: I'm filing a report, Clara. The buoy, and 1974. I'm sorry.
options.reply: ...I understand.

evening_d7.text: Light's on. The relief boat's due at first light. I suppose you've decided.
evening_d7.speaker: clara

options.text: I'm sending the tapes to June's family anyway.
options.reply: Then do it. I won't stop you.

options.text: I'm filing a report, Clara.

end_a_high.text: Goodnight, Arthur. Thank you, for all of it. Get some sleep before the boat.
end_a_high.speaker: clara

end_a_mid.text: Goodnight, Arthur. I'll be on sixteen at first light.
end_a_mid.speaker: clara

end_b.text: I've cut the supply. It'll go quiet by morning. Goodnight, Arthur.
end_b.speaker: clara

ending_a_radio.text: I have the relief boat on my board, Arthur. Wave to them for me. And thank you.
ending_a_radio.speaker: clara

ending_a_radio.text: The relief boat's on my board. Safe home, Arthur.
ending_a_radio.speaker: clara

ending_a_radio.text: Relief boat's on the board. Safe home.
ending_a_radio.speaker: clara

ending_b_radio.text: It's gone quiet, Arthur. I can't hear the ping any more. ...I have the relief boat on my board.
ending_b_radio.speaker: clara

ending_c_radio.text: Penobscot, Gannet Rock. Penobscot, Gannet Rock. ...Only static on sixteen.
ending_c_radio.speaker: arthur

lighthouse.text: I see your beam sweeping clear through the fog bank, Arthur. Clockwork weights holding steady?
lighthouse.speaker: clara

options.text: Wound an hour ago. The lens is turning smooth.
options.reply: Good. Keep an eye on the tide chart. Low water should expose the outer bars right about now.

options.text: Fog you could lean on, and the lamp's cutting through it anyway.
options.reply: That's what she's for. Stay off the sandbars once the tide turns.

cottage.text: Sounds warm in there. Did you find the spare kerosene cans in the stone shed?
cottage.speaker: clara

options.text: Stove's lit, coffee's on, fuel's plentiful.
options.reply: Jealous. All I've got is burnt machine coffee and static on channel 16.

options.text: Found some old 1970s oceanography logs on the shelf.
options.reply: Huh. Yeah, the university had the rock before automation. Weather balloons, drift buoys, that kind of thing.

sandbar_warning.text: Watch in your hand, Arthur, not your pocket. Make it back before the tide does.
sandbar_warning.speaker: clara

swept.text: Arthur! My tide monitor spiked. Did you just get cut off on the sandbar?
swept.speaker: clara

options.text: Back on the dock. Wet to the knees and rather embarrassed.
options.reply: Embarrassed is fine. Embarrassed is alive. Once the water tops two meters those bars are no place to be.

options.text: I'm fine. The water came in faster than the chart said.
options.reply: It always does. The chart's an average; the sea isn't. Wait for falling water before you cross again.

dusk_nudge.text: Light's going, Arthur. Stay on high ground and get that lamp lit.
dusk_nudge.speaker: clara

forced_home.text: Dark and bitter out there. Get in by the stove, Arthur. The rock will keep till morning.
forced_home.speaker: clara

lines.text: [Click. Wind in a stone cave. Somewhere deeper in, water moves against rock.]
June. It's the nineteenth of January, nineteen seventy-six. I'm in the west cave, at your buoy, because I couldn't think of anywhere else to put you.
I tried the cottage. I set the machine on the kitchen table, and every evening I sat down to tell you about my day, and every evening I found I'd been talking to the stove for an hour.
You used to say the only thing I ever said into a microphone was "Is this on?" [A short, unsteady laugh.] Well. It's on.
The Navy men left on the Tuesday boat. They took the good coffee, and the good chairs, and the cable charts. They left me a box of paperwork and a letter.
I'll read you the letter. "The Department regrets the loss of Mrs. June Haskell, civilian contractor, lost at sea in weather on the fourth of November, nineteen seventy-four. Mrs.
Haskell does not appear on the manifest for that date. No cable work was scheduled."
You never went to sea in your life, June. You went to the reef, with a red toolbag and an egg sandwich, and I watched you go.
I've read that letter four times. I read it to the stove. The stove had no opinion either.
The array's finished, they say. The cable stays in the ground, because that's cheaper than pulling it. Lieutenant Hayes signed that line himself. He has beautiful handwriting.
[Water drips. Walt breathes out.] I walked out at low water to see whether your buoy had gone dead, the way they promised. It hasn't. It's warm as a loaf, June.
I put my hand on the casing and it's warm.
And every fourteen seconds, listen, it picks up something off the reef.
[A faint electronic ping, very far off.]
[Under his breath.] ...nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen...
[A second ping, exactly where he said it would be.]
I asked Hayes what it was. He said a test tone. I said a test of what, now the array's finished? He said I wouldn't follow it. He's right about that. I don't.
I'm going to leave this in the hatch with the battery, where it's dry. I can't keep it at the cottage. If I keep it I'll play it every night, and then I'll have nothing new to say to you.
Goodnight, June. [A long breath.] I'll bring you the next one at the thaw. [Click.]
[Click. A hollow, ringing space. Dripping water. Boots on iron rungs.]
Field recorder, J. Haskell. Fourth of November, nineteen seventy-four. Oh-six-fifty-five, give or take my watch. Cable vault, south reef, splice number two.
Splice two has been dropping signal for a week. The Navy wants it sealed before the weather turns, and the weather is turning, so here I am, talking to a tape recorder in a concrete box.
For the record, the vault rings. I'm getting nearly two seconds of decay off these walls. Which is lovely, and no use to anyone.
The table gives me an hour of low water. Lieutenant Hayes says the Navy's schedule gives two. I'm going with the table. Walt, if you're listening to this over your coffee: I know. I know.
I copied it onto the card, same as you do every morning.
The technician's gone up. Poor lad hated the dark. The hatch seal's salt-crusted solid, I had to put my whole weight on the wheel, and the whole place smells of iron and old rope.
[She works. A ratchet clicks, stops, clicks. Her breath, steady.]
My fingers have stopped being useful. Egg again, Walt. Too much pepper again. It's the only warm thing I've eaten all day, so I've forgiven you.
[Water against the hatch. A sound like a hand laid flat on iron.] That's... earlier than the table said.
The vault sits lower than the bar. I should have put that on the card. And there's a swell under it from the south-east, I can hear the room change. Well.
Four minutes. The splice is nearly sealed. I'll finish, and I'll be out before it matters.
If this recorder ends up on someone else's shelf, tell Walt: the left pocket. He'll know. And tell him I wasn't careless. I read the card.
[The hatch clangs. Static.]
[Click. A kettle ticking as it cools. The wind is down. The room is small and close.]
June. Three years, near enough. I'm doing this one in the cottage. I've stopped taking them to the cave.
The Navy sends a man twice a year to look at your buoy now, and I'd rather he found a battery and nothing else.
A man came on the Tuesday boat with a briefcase. A commander. I didn't catch the name, which I expect was the idea. Very polite. He took his cap off in the kitchen.
He had a settlement. Four pages, and a fifth for my signature. A pension. A letter saying the Navy regrets. And one line, near the bottom, about not discussing the matter.
I asked him what I'd be not discussing. He said the schedule. I said, what schedule? He said it was classified.
So there was a schedule. [A dry breath.] I said, your schedule gave her two hours at the reef, and the table gave her one. And he didn't say a word, June. I've never been so glad of a man's silence.
I said Tom Dunmore ferried her out, and Tom says one hour. He said Tom was mistaken. He said it kindly. That's the part I can't forgive. He said it kindly.
I didn't sign. I turned the fifth page face down on the table and gave him a cup of tea, because he'd come a long way, and he drank it, and he left on the same boat.
Ruth writes. Your sister. She wrote again last week, from Providence. Every letter asks me the same thing: what did June say, the last time you saw her? And every time I put the pen down.
It was "don't wait up." That's what you said, at the landing, with your toolbag. Don't wait up. [Pause.] And I waited all night with the lamp and the radio, and nobody told me anything until noon.
I don't know how to put that in a letter to a woman who loved you nearly as much as I did.
I'll answer her. I will. Some day I'll put these in an envelope and Ruth can hear it all, the Navy and the tea and me. But not tonight. The kettle's gone cold.
Goodnight, June. [Click.]
[Click. The tape wanders a little. A door bangs somewhere in a draught. Wind, high up, against round glass.]
Whoever you are, you've found the locker. Good. Then you've found the lamp room, so I'll say what I'd have wanted said to me.
The lamp's easy once you know her. Wind the weights before you've had your coffee and she'll never let you down. Trim the wick. Never trust the third stair.
And when the fog comes down, listen for the bells before you look for the beam.
I'm leaving the rock tomorrow. Five winters. June would say that's four too many, and she'd be right, and she'd also be the one who stayed.
There are tapes. They're all addressed to her, so forgive the tone. There's one in the cave buoy and one under the bed, if you haven't found them. Listen in order, if you can bear it.
I made them in an order.
I've tried to post them to Ruth Whitcomb eleven times. Wickenden Street, Providence. June's sister. The only person who ever asked me how I was.
I stand at the post office window with the envelope, and I think, she'll hear me grieving, and I'd rather she heard June.
So they're here. If you've a steadier hand than mine, take them to her.
Tom Dunmore left something in the cove hut for me, years ago. A tin, on a crate. I never could bring myself to play it. If you've a stronger stomach than I have, it's yours.
A voice on sixteen asks after me at ten every night. Whoever has the watch. Never more than the weather, and never more than I answer. [A short breath.]
Two grown men, a radio, the same night on both our minds, and neither of us asks the one thing.
Don't do what I did. If somebody's out there, answer them. Talk to a person. A machine is a poor place to keep a life.
The buoy in the cave is still ticking. I don't know who feeds it. Leave it be. Maybe someone needs it more than I did.
[A long pause. The door bangs once.] Mind your head on the gallery door. Goodnight. [Click.]

tape_5.title: Tape 5: Boatswain T. Dunmore, boat log

lines.text: [Click. A diesel engine idling. Gulls. A man clears his throat.]
Boat log. Coast Guard, Gannet Rock run. Monday, fourth of November, nineteen seventy-four. Oh-five-forty. Landed the Pelagic party at the south reef causeway. Mrs.
Haskell, one technician, Lieutenant Hayes.
Wind south-east, rising. Swell building. The table has the bar dry from oh-six-ten to about oh-seven-ten. One hour.
I told the lieutenant. He said the Navy's schedule gave two. I said the table's the table, sir. I said the vault sits lower than the bar and goes under first. He said, noted.
Oh-six-fifty. The technician has come off the reef. Mrs. Haskell has stayed to finish the splice. The lieutenant says she has her time.
Oh-seven-oh-five. Water making on the bar, early, with the swell behind it. I'm holding station off the reef with the engine running. I can see her lamp in the hatch glass.
Oh-seven-ten. Hailing the hatch. No answer. [His voice drops.] Hailing the hatch. Oh God. I can't get in over the bar. The swell's too heavy.
[A pause. Only the engine.]
Oh-seven-twenty-one. Her lamp has gone out.
[A long silence.] This isn't going in the report. The lieutenant is writing his own. I'll say it here instead, for whoever finds it. I said one hour.
Boatswain T. Dunmore, signing off. [A long breath.] I've a girl at home who's four. She'll ask me tonight what I did at work. [Click.]
[Click. Wind in a cave. Metal on stone. A woman close to the microphone, a little out of breath.]
Dad. It's me. I'm in the cave again. I've swapped the battery. It's good for another winter, if the cold holds.
I signed it out as a spare for the Penobscot repeater. Don't laugh. If anyone counts, I'll go to prison for a battery.
I know what you'd say. You'd say leave it. You told me once the sea owed you something, and I've never known if you meant it as a debt or a warning.
The hydrophone picks up a ping every fourteen seconds, from the reef. Every one. I've timed it against the console clock. I tell myself it's her recorder. [Quieter.] I know it isn't.
The recorder's been dead since before I could read. It's the splice transponder, doing exactly what it was built to do.
But if I stop listening, Dad, then nobody is. Somebody has to be listening.
Walt's tape is still in the main hatch. I've never taken it out. It felt like reading his mail, and it felt like putting him out of the room.
So I'll leave mine here, under the service hatch, with the old battery. I can't keep it at the flat. It's too loud in there.
They're sending someone out for the winter. A man on his own, I heard. I hope it's someone who minds his own business. [A short laugh.] I'll be on sixteen at ten, like always.
That's all he'll get from me.
I'm twenty-seven years old, and I talk to a cave. It'll be three years in December.
[A breath.] I miss you. [Click.]
